title: 1. Origin, Corporate Evolution & Past Business Cycles
book_title: Chapter 1: How the Business Got Here — From Oil Seismographs to 300mm Analog Dominance

epigraph.quote: We don't manage the company for next quarter's utilization rate; we build manufacturing capacity that will still be compounding per-share cash flow twenty years from now.
epigraph.author: Texas Instruments Capital Management Philosophy

web_blocks.html: Texas Instruments Incorporated (TI) has reinvented itself several times over nearly a century [1, 7]. Along the way, it shed lower-return units to focus on one durable economic engine [1, 7]. The company began in 1930 as Geophysical Service Incorporated (GSI), using reflection seismographs to find oil [7]. During World War II, it shifted into defense gear and adopted the name Texas Instruments in 1951 [7]. That engineering culture produced two landmark breakthroughs in modern electronics. TI built the first commercial silicon transistor in 1954, and Jack Kilby demonstrated the integrated circuit (IC) in 1958 [7]. Yet for today's investors, TI's defining moves were not its 1950s inventions. They were the disciplined portfolio exits executed between 1995 and 2012.

For decades, TI ran as a sprawling defense and chip conglomerate. It made military radar, consumer calculators, laptops, DRAM memory chips, and OMAP phone processors [7]. Every one of those units shared a fatal flaw. They suffered from short product lives, heavy buyer concentration, or steep Moore's Law spending that eroded returns every few years. Under CEOs Tom Engibous and Rich Templeton, TI exited those traps step by step [7]. It sold defense electronics to Raytheon in 1997 and DRAM memory to Micron in 1998 [7]. It divested sensors and controls in 2006, then wound down its OMAP wireless unit in 2012 [7]. Management shifted capital and engineers into Analog and Embedded Processing. In these fragmented markets, a single chip win in a factory drive or car powertrain can ship for 10 to 20 years.

The biggest deal in that pivot came in 2011, when TI bought National Semiconductor for $6.5 billion [7]. That purchase added about 12,000 analog parts and deepened TI's power-management and signal-chain catalog. It also set a clear template for buying assets during slowdowns. Ten years later, in 2021, TI applied the same playbook to wafer fabs. It bought Micron Technology's 300mm fab in Lehi, Utah (LFAB1) for $900 million [4, 7]. That deal secured cleanroom space at a fraction of new-build cost [4, 7]. In April 2023, Rich Templeton handed the CEO role to Haviv Ilan [4, 7]. Ilan was a 24-year TI veteran who had run Analog, Embedded Processing, and the 2022–2026 300mm buildout plan [4, 7].

web_blocks.takeaway: TI spent 25 years pruning short-cycle, capital-hungry businesses to concentrate on long-lifecycle Analog and Embedded chips, then used the 2022–2025 cycle to lock in a generational 300mm U.S. manufacturing footprint.

web_blocks.html: To read TI's recent results, you must separate the demand cycle from the factory-build cycle. During the 2020–2022 chip shortage, TI's revenue jumped to $18,344 million in 2021 and $20,028 million in 2022 [7]. In 2022, operating profit reached $10,487 million and free cash flow hit $5,923 million [7]. Then came the post-pandemic inventory glut. Industrial and auto buyers spent 2023 and 2024 working down excess part stockpiles. TI's revenue fell 12.5% to $17,519 million in 2023, then dropped another 10.7% to $15,641 million in 2024 [1, 7]. Operating profit fell by nearly half from its 2022 peak to $5,350 million in 2024 [1, 7].

Most chipmakers slash capital spending when sales drop 22% from peak to trough. TI did the exact opposite. Management bet that U.S. supply security and 300mm wafer math would shape the next twenty years. It pushed gross capex to $5,071 million in 2023, $4,820 million in 2024, and $4,550 million in 2025 [1, 7]. As a result, free cash flow shrank from $6,294 million in 2021 to $1,349 million in 2023 and $1,498 million in 2024 [1, 7]. At the same time, TI raised internal inventory from ~$2 billion pre-pandemic to $4,804 million by year-end 2025 [1]. That 222-day buffer let TI ship parts right away when buyers returned [1].

By 2026, that twin bet on 300mm capacity and ready stock began to pay off. Revenue grew 13.0% in 2025 to $17,682 million [1]. Growth sped up through 2026, hitting $4,825 million in Q1, $5,463 million in Q2, and $6,055 million in Q3 [2, 3]. That Q3 figure rose 28% year-over-year and topped the prior 2022 quarterly peak [2, 3]. Gross margin climbed from 57.0% in FY2025 to 64.2% in Q3 2026 as fab load rose and Sherman's SM1 fab started output [1, 2, 4]. On February 4, 2026, TI also announced an all-cash deal to buy Silicon Labs for about $7.5 billion in enterprise value [6]. The deal targets a first-half 2027 close and adds ~1,200 wireless parts to Embedded Processing [6].

Why Analog Lifecycles Reward Patient Capital: Consumer logic and memory chips often turn obsolete within 24 months. By contrast, TI builds analog and embedded parts on mature nodes from 28nm to 130nm [4, 7]. Products on those nodes often stay in production for 10 to 20 years [4, 7]. An industrial motor drive or car battery system takes years of safety testing to qualify. Once TI wins a socket, the revenue stream acts like a long-term royalty. That long life is why building 300mm cleanrooms during a downturn makes economic sense. Fabs built in 2023–2025 will still stamp out high-margin chips in 2040 [4].

Capital Discipline Across Three Decades: TI's shift from a broad conglomerate to a focused analog supplier did not happen by chance. Each divestiture removed a unit that demanded constant node shrinks or relied on one or two large buyers. In wireless basebands, a single phone cycle could wipe out two years of R&D work. In DRAM, industry oversupply crushed margins every few years regardless of execution. By leaving those markets, TI freed cash to buy National Semiconductor and build its 300mm U.S. fabs. That multi-decade focus explains why TI can spend $14.4 billion across 2023–2025 without losing its balance-sheet footing [1, 7].

web_blocks.mechanism: During severe downturns, blast-furnace rivals froze spending and shut plants. Nucor invested through the trough in electric-arc mini-mills and thin-slab casting. It accepted lower near-term cash flow to secure a lasting cost edge.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: Nucor's per-ton conversion cost fell ~25%–35% below integrated peers. It stayed profitable across recessions and earned over 15% ROIC across full steel cycles while rivals restructured.
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: Like Nucor, TI used the 2023–2024 analog slump to build 300mm fabs (RFAB2, SM1/SM2, LFAB2) with ~40% lower die cost than 200mm fabs. Lower near-term FCF during the build is the deliberate price for margin leadership in the recovery.

web_blocks.title: THE CYCLE LESSON
paragraphs: Do not confuse an inventory slump with product decay, or peak-capex cash flow with normal earning power. TI's 2023–2025 numbers looked tight because it ran a $14.4B fab buildout through a 22% sales drop. The real test now is whether 2026–2028 sales growth and lower capex lift FCF per share without leaving idle fabs.

book_paragraphs: To understand Texas Instruments, start by dropping the myth that it is a typical Silicon Valley chipmaker. TI began in Dallas in 1930 as Geophysical Service Incorporated, using reflection seismographs to hunt for oil. Trace its path from oil-field gear to defense radar, to the 1954 silicon transistor and Jack Kilby's 1958 integrated circuit. You quickly see a culture built on physical factories and long-term engineering, not consumer hype.

Yet the defining chapter in TI's modern story is not what it invented. It is what leadership had the grit to quit. By the mid-1990s, TI was a sprawling conglomerate making defense gear, laptops, DRAM memory, and OMAP phone chips. Every one of those units carried a hidden trap for long-term compounding. Either you stayed on a Moore's Law treadmill where factories aged out every two years, or you depended on one or two phone giants who could drop you overnight.

Between 1997 and 2012, TI's leaders took that conglomerate apart piece by piece. They sold defense to Raytheon, DRAM to Micron, and sensors to Bain Capital, then shut down OMAP wireless chips. Every dollar of cash and engineering talent went into two sticky, fragmented markets: Analog and Embedded Processing. In 2011, TI doubled down by buying National Semiconductor for $6.5 billion, building the widest analog catalog in the industry.

Picture what happens when you own 80,000 specialized chips that sell for fifty cents to five dollars each. They sit inside factory robots, plant sensors, and car powertrains. Once an engineer designs your power chip onto a board, that part can ship unchanged for ten to twenty years. Nobody swaps out a proven $1.20 voltage regulator to save three cents when a failure could recall a million cars.

book_subsections.title: The 2022–2026 Counter-Cyclical Bet
paragraphs: That brings us to the cycle we are studying right now. Coming out of the pandemic shortage, TI's revenue peaked at $20.03 billion in 2022, with $10.49 billion in operating profit. Then factory and auto buyers realized they had ordered too much. A two-year inventory burn began. Sales fell to $17.52 billion in 2023 and $15.64 billion in 2024, while operating profit nearly halved to $5.35 billion.

At most chip firms, management would have panicked, halted construction, and cut plant staff to defend quarterly margins. Under CEO Haviv Ilan, who succeeded Rich Templeton in April 2023, TI did the reverse. It kept building 300mm wafer fabs across Richardson and Sherman in Texas and Lehi in Utah. Capex hit $5.07 billion in 2023, $4.82 billion in 2024, and $4.55 billion in 2025. Free cash flow fell from $6.29 billion in 2021 to just $1.35 billion in 2023.

By 2026, that contrarian bet began to show up in the numbers. Revenue rebounded to $17.68 billion in 2025, then accelerated through 2026. Sales hit $4.83 billion in Q1, $5.46 billion in Q2, and $6.06 billion in Q3 2026, up 28% year-over-year. Gross margin jumped from 57.0% in 2025 to 64.2% in Q3 2026 as factories filled up and Sherman's SM1 fab started production. In February 2026, TI also announced a $7.5 billion cash deal for Silicon Labs to expand its wireless Embedded lineup. The demand cycle and the capex cycle are now crossing in the right direction.

Look closely at what sets TI's capital cycle apart from a commodity chipmaker. In DRAM or NAND memory, every upturn sparks a building race. Rivals put up identical leading-edge fabs that turn obsolete in three years, wrecking returns. In analog and embedded chips, nodes live at 28 nanometers to 130 nanometers for twenty years or more. Once TI pours concrete in Sherman or Richardson and qualifies its 300mm lines, those cleanrooms can stamp out chips for decades with very little fresh R&D.

That is why the Nucor Steel parallel fits so well. When Nucor built electric-arc mini-mills during steel slumps, Wall Street hated the near-term cash drain. Yet once demand returned, Nucor's low cost floor let it earn strong returns across the cycle while legacy mills bled. TI spent four years building the chip world's version of those mini-mills. In 2026, the operating leverage from that choice is finally hitting the income statement.

book_subsections.title: Why Portfolio Pruning Mattered More Than Any Single Invention
paragraphs: It is easy to praise Jack Kilby's 1958 integrated circuit. Yet for a modern investor, Tom Engibous and Rich Templeton's decision to shrink TI's footprint between 1997 and 2012 mattered even more. Exiting defense, DRAM, sensors, and OMAP phone chips meant giving up billions in headline sales. Many CEOs refuse that trade because smaller top-line revenue hurts executive pride.

By accepting short-term exits, TI escaped Moore's Law capex inflation and single-buyer risk. When Apple or Samsung redesigned a phone every twelve months, suppliers lived on a knife-edge. By pivoting into 80,000 long-life analog and embedded parts sold to over 100,000 industrial and auto buyers, TI turned a volatile hardware firm into a steady cash engine.

That patient culture also shapes how TI handles leadership changes. Haviv Ilan worked inside the company for over twenty years before taking over from Rich Templeton in April 2023. He helped design the 2022–2026 300mm capacity plan long before he became CEO. Many tech firms rip up their strategy every time a new chief arrives. At TI, the core playbook—300mm cost leadership, direct TI.com sales, and long-term growth in free cash flow per share—has stayed steady across multiple leadership teams.

Inventory strategy followed the same patient logic. While peers dumped stock and cut shifts in 2023, TI built its buffer to $4.80 billion, or 222 days of supply, by late 2025. Because analog parts do not spoil or age out like phone processors, holding extra wafers carried very low write-off risk. When industrial buyers came back with rush orders in 2026, TI had parts on the shelf and captured share right away.

That same discipline shows up in how TI treats acquisitions. After buying National Semiconductor in 2011 for $6.5 billion, TI spent fifteen years focusing on organic 300mm fab construction rather than chasing trophy deals. Only after its Texas and Utah cleanroom shells were built did management step up for the $7.5 billion Silicon Labs acquisition in February 2026. Every major capital move across thirty years—from exiting DRAM in 1998 to buying Micron's Lehi fab in 2021—followed one simple rule: own long-lived analog and embedded assets at the lowest possible unit cost.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: The hardest move for any public-company CEO is spending $14.4 billion on plants while sales fall 22%. That is what TI did from 2023 through 2025. Whether that proves brilliant or excessive rests on two tests we will audit next: the unit-cost math of 300mm wafers, and normal cash flow once capex drops to $2–$3 billion.
